narrative: The model estimates a 78% probability that you will leave your job, so it flags you as a high retention risk; that is why the promotion decision came out as denied. In practical terms, this is not a judgment of your performance, but a warning that your profile resembles employees who tend to exit. The strongest signal was your total work experience: at 6–10 years, you fall into a group the model associates with leaving more than the more common 1–5 year group among employees predicted to stay. The second strongest signal was your tenure with your current organization: 1–5 years here also pushed the prediction toward leaving, especially alongside your broader experience. The third signal, having no other job opportunities, actually pushed toward staying, but it was not strong enough to offset the first two. Other factors, such as low emotional commitment, no annual bonus, no medical insurance, low job stability, and low satisfaction, add concern but ranked below the top three. Next, you and the organization should treat this as a retention conversation: clarify what would make the role sustainable and worth staying in, review development and promotion pathways, address recognition, support, and rewards, and agree on concrete milestones. A promotion decision should rest on performance and readiness, while this risk signal should prompt support, not be the only reason for denial.
